questions.stem: Calculate the time complexity of merge sort for a list of 1024 elements. Provide your answer in $O$ notation.
questions.explanation: Merge sort has a time complexity of $O(n \log n)$. For $n = 1024$, $\log_2(1024) = 10$, so the complexity is $O(1024 \times 10) = O(10240)$. However, in $O$ notation, constants are ignored, so the answer is $O(n \log n)$.

questions.stem: Explain how the divide-and-conquer paradigm is applied in merge sort and how it contributes to its efficiency.
markingGuide: Divide step: splitting the list into two halves.
Conquer step: recursively sorting each half.
Efficiency from solving smaller subproblems and merging in linear time.
questions.explanation: The divide-and-conquer paradigm in merge sort involves dividing the list into two halves, recursively sorting each half, and merging the sorted halves. This approach allows merge sort to efficiently handle large datasets by breaking the problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems. The merging process, which is linear, ensures that the overall time complexity remains $O(n \log n)$.

questions.stem: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using merge sort compared to quicksort.
markingGuide: Merge sort is stable, quicksort is not.
Merge sort has consistent $O(n \log n)$ time complexity.
Quicksort has better average-case performance but worse worst-case performance.
Merge sort requires additional space, quicksort is in-place.
questions.explanation: Merge sort is stable and has a consistent time complexity of $O(n \log n)$, making it predictable in performance. However, it requires additional space for merging. Quicksort, on the other hand, is not stable and has a worst-case time complexity of $O(n^2)$, though it often performs better in practice due to its in-place sorting nature.
